newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel-PLO summit not on agenda, Arafat says.
newsitem.headline: Israel-PLO summit not on agenda, Arafat says.

text.p: Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat said on Wednesday there was no prospect of a summit with Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu to break a two-month-old peace deadlock

He spoke to reporters after a 90-minute meeting with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak's envoy, Osama al-Baz, who reported to him on an Israeli-Egyptian summit on Tuesday aimed at reviving peacemaking.
Asked if he had agreed to meet Netanyahu in a bid to revive the talks stalled over Jewish settlement construction in the West Bank, Arafat said: "There is no such offer."
Mubarak said after meeting Netanyahu on Tuesday he hoped soon to bring the Palestinian leader into a three-way meeting.
A halt to Jewish settlement expansion, including in Arab East Jerusalem, is Arafat's condition for resuming talks with Israel but Netanyahu rules it out.
Netanyahu's groundbreaking in March on a Jerusalem settlement, known as Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic, brought peace talks to a standstill.
Asked if Israel had agreed to halt settlement construction, Arafat said: "Not yet. This subject is not done yet." He accused Israel of violating peace accords.
The Israeli and Egyptian leaders, their countries partners to a 1979 treaty, said their summit in the Egyptian resort of Sharm el-Sheikh would be followed by more talks on ending the crisis.
After meeting Arafat, al-Baz said: "We are moving on certain steps and we can't reach an understanding in one step."
Arafat's adviser Ahmed Tibi told Israel's army radio on Wednesday: "The crisis situation still exists. The ball is still in Mr Netanyahu's court."
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said Cairo would await Netanyahu's response to issues raised at the summit before al-Baz shuttles between Israel and the Palestinians.

"Good will on Israel's part isn't enough to renew the peace talks. The Palestinians cannot accept a continuation of settlement activity -- and primarily in Jerusalem -- as a good will gesture," Moussa told Israel's Haaretz newspaper.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy declined comment on whether his country would accept a settlement freeze.

But he told the radio on Wednesday: "I will say with certainty that if anyone expected Israel to come to Sharm el-Sheikh to accept all that was dictated to it, that did not happen and won't happen. If anyone thinks Israel will come and like a sphinx stand and say 'I have no alternative proposals', he too will be disappointed."

Levy said Netanyahu's inner security cabinet was on Wednesday holding its first of many discussions on its vision of a final peace deal with Palestinians. That accord, due to be completed in two years, will deal with the toughest issues such as borders, Jerusalem, settlements and Palestinian refugees.
